e: AWS Step Functions orchestrates serverless workflows as state machines that invoke Lambda functions, which is event-driven, distributed, and low-overhead. Glue is for ETL, EC2 adds server management, and EventBridge schedules aren't workflow orchestration.

AWS Global Accelerator supports UDP listeners and routes users over the AWS global network to the closest healthy regional endpoint, reducing latency and packet loss. CloudFront doesn't support UDP, and Transit Gateway or VPC peering aren't user-facing accelerators.

RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ is fully managed, highly available, and fault tolerant. 1,000 IOPS (2,000 with headroom) on a 1 TB volume is well within what gp2 delivers (3 IOPS per GB, about 3,000 baseline), so gp2 is far cheaper than io2 Block Express. S3 Intelligent-Tiering isn't a database, and self-managed EC2 isn't fully managed.

RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections so Lambda's bursty concurrency doesn't exhaust the database, with minimal code change (just the endpoint). Lowering concurrency hurts the application, and resizing or migrating to DynamoDB doesn't address connection handling as simply.

AWS Batch on EC2 can run the job on a large instance with 64 vCPU and 512 GiB, completing it within the 15 minutes, and manages the compute environment and job queueing. Lambda is limited to 10 GB memory and 15-minute runtime with 6 vCPU, and Fargate and Lightsail don't offer that size.

S3 Standard-IA lowers storage cost for rarely accessed data while keeping immediate (millisecond) access and the same multi-AZ availability and resiliency. Glacier Deep Archive isn't immediately accessible, and One Zone-IA stores data in one AZ, reducing resiliency (and can't be applied before 30 days).

Static files in S3 with CloudFront caching give highly available, low-latency delivery. Windows Server instances need shared storage for server-side code, and FSx for Windows File Server provides a highly available SMB share they can all mount. EFS isn't supported on Windows, and EBS volumes can't be shared across instances.

A Lambda@Edge function attached to the CloudFront behaviors can resize images on the fly and choose the format (such as WebP) per request, serverless and scaling automatically. Origin request or response header policies can't process images, and EC2-based processing needs management.

The aws:SecureTransport condition enforces encryption in transit, and SSE-KMS with customer managed keys lets the compliance team administer the keys through the key policy. SSE-S3 keys are managed by AWS, ACM certificates don't attach to S3, and Macie only detects sensitive data.

An interface VPC endpoint for API Gateway (execute-api) keeps API-to-API calls inside the VPC through PrivateLink with almost no code change. Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, and API keys or SQS don't change the network path.

DynamoDB with DAX provides sub-millisecond reads for hot data, and DynamoDB table export to S3 plus Athena lets you run one-time queries on historical data with little operational work. RDS can't offer sub-millisecond reads, and the other options add custom scripts or don't give fast reads.

SQS FIFO queues preserve message order within a message group, so using the payment ID as the group ID keeps each payment's messages ordered. Kinesis data streams preserve order within a shard, and using the payment ID as the partition key routes a payment's records to the same shard. Standard SQS, DynamoDB, and Memcached don't guarantee ordered delivery.

SNS FIFO topics preserve order and fan out each event to multiple subscribers (the leaderboard, matchmaking, and authentication services, each typically through its own SQS FIFO queue) concurrently. A single SQS FIFO queue delivers to one consumer group, and EventBridge and standard SNS don't guarantee ordering.

Enable SSE on SQS using a customer managed KMS key, restrict who can use the key, and add a queue policy condition requiring TLS (aws:SecureTransport) to encrypt in transit. The IAM policy variant also restricts usage of the key, so both D and E satisfy these needs. (Options A and C use the default key policy, and B lacks a TLS condition.)

RDS automated backups with transaction logs enable point-in-time recovery to any second within the retention period (up to 35 days), covering 5 minutes before the change within 30 days. Manual snapshots are point-in-time only, and read replicas and Multi-AZ replicate the bad edit too.

Cognito user pools can carry subscription claims or groups, and fine-grained IAM permissions (for example, through an identity pool role or condition keys on DynamoDB) can restrict premium content to subscribed users with minimal operational overhead. Caching, WAF, and usage plans with API keys don't identify subscribed users.

Network Load Balancers support UDP, and Global Accelerator can use NLB endpoints (which can address on-premises IPs) to route users over the AWS network to the nearest healthy site, improving performance and availability. ALBs don't support UDP, and CloudFront doesn't support UDP.
IAM password policies are set once at the account level and apply to all IAM users, including complexity and mandatory rotation (maximum age). There is no per-user password policy.

AWS Batch runs the tasks as containerized or scripted jobs of any language, scales compute automatically, and EventBridge schedules them, with little operational overhead. Lambda's 15-minute limit rules out 1-hour tasks, and App Runner is for web services.

A NAT gateway is the managed option (a NAT instance is self-managed), and it must sit in a public subnet with the private subnets' default route pointing to it so private instances can reach the internet. A NAT in a private subnet can't reach the internet gateway.

Enabling EBS encryption by default with the customer managed key makes all new volumes (including the node group's) use that key, and the EKS cluster's IAM role needs permissions on the key to let the nodes' volumes use it. This avoids manual re-encryption or plugins.

Store large images in S3 (cheap, scalable, highly available) and keep the geographic code to S3 URL mapping in DynamoDB, which scales for tens of thousands of updates every few minutes. Items in DynamoDB are limited to 400 KB, so high-resolution images don't fit, and Oracle on RDS costs more.

Intelligent-Tiering automatically handles the changing access patterns for the 30-day and 12-month retrains, with data always available with minimal delay, and a lifecycle policy then transitions objects to Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year for archival. (The Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers aren't set up to move to Deep Archive on that schedule as in B.)

One Direct Connect connection with a transit gateway attached to the three VPCs gives consistent, high-throughput, low-latency connectivity to the on-premises application and VPC-to-VPC communication at the lowest cost. VPN lacks consistent performance, and three Direct Connect connections cost more.

AWS Step Functions orchestrates Lambda functions and also services on EC2, containers, and on-premises, and supports manual approval steps (callback patterns), with low operational overhead. Glue, SQS, or hand-built EventBridge flows lack workflow orchestration.
